title: Can Generate–Validate–Repair Reduce Unsafe LLM‑Generated Network Configurations? A Paired, Validator‑Grounded Study
abstract: We evaluate whether a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces executable unsafe network configurations produced from natural‑language intents. Under a preregistered paired design (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) we produced exactly one LLM sample per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics) using gpt‑5‑mini, reused that candidate for both baseline and guarded conditions, and applied a deterministic network validator with a single permitted automated repair. Results (N=200 paired intents): baseline valid = 200/200 (100%), guarded valid = 200/200 (100%); paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; 95% paired bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). No repairs were applied because all shared initial candidates were validator‑valid. Important clarifier: because the executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one sampled candidate deterministically reused across arms), the estimand measures only downstream validator/repair effects on a fixed initial candidate and does NOT measure effects arising from independent per‑condition sampling, different prompting, or sampling nondeterminism. The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling. We report complete preregistration, execution artifacts, and a focused discussion of threats to validity and practical next steps.

sections.introduction: Motivation and question. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate natural‑language intents into device configuration sequences for network operations (NetOps). However, hallucination and unsafe outputs undermine trust in operational applications and motivate verifier‑assisted pipelines that attempt to detect and repair unsafe outputs. We asked: Does a GVR pipeline—LLM generate, deterministic validator check, and a single automated repair attempt—reduce the rate of executable unsafe or incorrect network configurations relative to reusing the same LLM candidate without validator/repair? Design choice and rationale. We preregistered a paired design under shared_initial_candidate semantics so that each intent yields exactly one sampled candidate deterministically reused by baseline and guarded arms; this isolates the downstream effect of deterministic validation and an allowed repair on a fixed candidate (the estimand is therefore the paired post‑generation validator/repair effect). The design was chosen (and frozen in the preregistration) to separate downstream repair efficacy from sampling variability and to provide a tractable confirmatory test of the validator/repair mechanism under controlled conditions. Contributions. (1) a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment and full artifact capture; (2) a validator‑grounded, deterministic scoring analysis on N=200 paired intents using gpt‑5‑mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5; (3) transparent reporting of a null paired effect and a calibrated interpretation that explains why the experimental semantics produced that result.
sections.related_work: Verification, RAG, and verifier‑guided repair. Hallucination and reliability problems for LLMs are documented across domains and motivate evidence‑grounded generation and verification [1,2]. Retrieval‑ and evidence‑grounded designs can reduce hallucination in operations‑style QA tasks [2]. Verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair architectures have been proposed and demonstrated to improve correctness in infrastructure‑as‑code and related code‑generation tasks (e.g., TerraFormer) though primarily outside device‑level NetOps execution studies [3]. Prior NetOps LLM evaluations measure translation capability but not standardized execution‑level safety in packet‑level simulators [4]. The supplied literature therefore supports the plausibility of verifier‑guided improvements while leaving open transferability to executed network‑configuration safety; that gap motivated our preregistered confirmatory run.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. The experiment was preregistered as PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01 with a paired confirmatory design (N=200 paired intents). Sampling and tasks. We selected a deterministic task bank of 200 synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' intents prior to any model calls. Generation semantics and model. Execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for baseline and guarded episodes. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution manifest: model_calls_used = 200). The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validator and repair. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 produced binary valid/invalid labels and, for guarded episodes, a single automated repair attempt was permitted if the validator flagged violations. Scoring and estimand. Primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (per‑intent executable validity). Primary test: exact two‑sided McNemar on the paired 2×2 table; we report exact p‑values and the absolute risk difference with 95% paired bootstrap percentile CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10000). Analysis adhered to the preregistered complete_pair_primary policy and sensitivity plans. Important methodological note: under shared_initial_candidate semantics baseline vs guarded compare the same initial sampled candidate (unmodified) versus that candidate after deterministic validation/repair; independent first‑pass sampling per condition was not executed.
sections.results:
Execution and accounting. The hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter completed the preregistered run: planned_episode_count=400, completed_episode_count=400, failed_episode_count=0, model_calls_used=200 (one shared initial generation per intent). Scoring outcomes: baseline_success_count = 200/200 (100%), guarded_success_count = 200/200 (100%). Paired contingency table: n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; paired difference = 0.0. Exact McNemar two‑sided test: p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap (seed=1729, 10,000 resamples) 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.0]. Repair activity: the validator reported no violations on any shared initial candidate; consequently no repair prompts were issued and no repairs were applied in guarded episodes. Representative validator excerpts (from archived artifacts): task‑000004 normalized_configuration = "interface edge2 admin down
interface edge2 vlan 40
interface edge2 admin up
interface edge1 admin down" with validator.valid = true; task‑000005 normalized_configuration = "interface uplink2 admin up
interface uplink1 admin down
interface uplink1 vlan 210" with validator.valid = true. All preregistered contamination and missingness checks passed; no pairs were excluded.
sections.discussion: Interpretation. The confirmatory null effect is a direct consequence of the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics combined with the observed data: the single sampled candidate per intent was validator‑valid in all 200 tasks, leaving no opportunity for the repair step to change outcomes. Scientifically this run (a) demonstrates a fully artifacted, reproducible GVR evaluation workflow with deterministic scoring, and (b) clarifies that paired designs which reuse one sampled candidate across arms cannot detect benefits that would arise from independent per‑condition sampling or alternative prompting. Threats to validity (selected). Internal: shared_initial_candidate semantics restrict the estimand to post‑generation validator/repair effects; archived model configuration shows temperature = null (unset), which is not evidence of deterministic sampling; single model/provider and single validator implementation limit inference. Construct: synthetic task bank and validator abstraction may not capture vendor CLI intricacies or runtime interactions. External: no live hardware/emulation and limited task diversity limit generalizability. Power and planning note. The preregistered power plan targeted an absolute improvement of ≈10 percentage points; the observed baseline 100% success rate made the confirmatory McNemar test uninformative for repair efficacy. This outcome suggests future confirmatory runs should (for example) use independent per‑condition sampling, higher sampling variance, adversarial or more challenging task subsets, or broader model diversity to create observable discordant pairs and thereby test repair efficacy. Practical implication. The run validates the end‑to‑end artifact pipeline while underscoring that experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate) must align with the scientific question: to measure repair impact on real sampling variability, independent first‑pass draws per condition are required.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment to test whether a GVR pipeline reduces executable unsafe LLM‑generated network configurations. In this run (N=200 pairs, shared_initial_candidate, gpt‑5‑mini) all initial candidates were validator‑valid and no repairs were applied; thus the guarded pipeline produced no measurable improvement relative to baseline (paired difference = 0.0, exact McNemar p = 1.0). The study establishes a reproducible, artifacted evaluation workflow and documents crucial experimental semantics (shared_initial_candidate; temperature recorded as null/unset) that constrain interpretation. Future work should evaluate independent sampling regimes, broaden model and task diversity, and increase validator fidelity to vendor and runtime behaviour. References: [1] P. Jana et al., "TerraFormer: Automated Infrastructure‑as‑Code with LLMs Fine‑Tuned via Policy‑Guided Verifier Feedback," 2026. [2] B. Zhang, H. Rao, D. Zhao, "Evidence‑Grounded RAG for Cloud‑Native DevOps: Hallucination‑Resistant AIOps Question Answering over Private Operations Documents," JACS, 2024. [3] A. Agarwal, "Adversarial Hallucination Engineering: Targeted Misdirection Attacks Against LLM Powered Security Operations Centers," preprint, 2025. [4] Y. Miao et al., "An Empirical Study of NetOps Capability of Pre‑Trained Large Language Models," arXiv:2309.05557, 2023.

disclosure_statement: Disclosure (concise): Human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) prior to the autonomy lock. After the lock the autonomous system performed literature review, experiment selection, preregistration (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01), code generation, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting without manual human editing of technical content. Declared model: gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter 'openai_responses' (execution used model_calls_used = 200). Generation semantics executed: shared_initial_candidate — exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline and guarded conditions (no independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling). The archived model configuration records temperature = null (unset); null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0. Validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 scored candidates and a single automated repair iteration was permitted; in this run the validator flagged no violations and no repairs were applied. Execution accounting: completed_episode_count = 400 (200 paired intents), completed without preregistration deviations. Master prompt immutable reference: provenance/master_prompt.txt — 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as empirical evidence in this final run. After the autonomy lock no human manually rewrote technical results, manuscript text, figures, or references.
limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: a single sampled initial generation was reused across baseline and guarded conditions; this design measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition first‑pass sampling or different prompting strategies.

Temperature unset (temperature=null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature=0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic intent_configuration_repair_v1 items with deterministic validator scoring; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed in live devices or exhaustive vendor emulators.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects task/sampling conditions rather than proof that GVR is unnecessary in general.

External validity: absence of live hardware/emulation execution and limited task diversity constrain operational generalizability; follow‑on studies should expand model diversity, sampling regimes, and validator fidelity.
